messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 65

John, a 63-year-old financial analyst of Oceania ethnicity, lives in constant vigilance since the life-threatening car accident that changed his life two years ago. Married to Sarah for over three decades, John’s once orderly and meticulous world now feels unpredictable and dangerous. The accident occurred on one of his regular commutes home from work; a drunk driver ran a red light, crashing into him head-on. Though he survived the crash with physical injuries that have since healed, the emotional scars continue to plague him. In the days following the accident, John struggled to sleep, plagued by vivid nightmares where he relives the moment of impact and the deafening screech of metal as his car crumpled under the force. He wakes up drenched in sweat, heart pounding, feeling as though he is suffocating under the weight of debris. These episodes have become so frequent that Sarah often finds him pacing their living room in the middle of the night, muttering to himself about staying alert and watching out for danger. At work, John’s performance has noticeably declined despite his rigorous efforts to maintain focus on financial reports and market analysis. His mind wanders back to the accident whenever a loud noise disrupts the office environment—a sudden burst from the printer or an abrupt slam of a door can send him into a panic. He jumps at every unexpected sound, imagining each one as a harbinger of another impending crash. Colleagues have noticed his heightened anxiety and withdrawal; he avoids taking on projects that require traveling to unfamiliar cities, fearing that another accident could happen again. John’s relationship with Sarah has also been strained by the changes in him. She finds it difficult to understand why her husband now seems so distant and guarded. In moments of vulnerability, John admits to feeling guilty for surviving when others didn’t. He wonders if he should have done something differently, if perhaps taking a different route home would have prevented the crash. This constant self-blame gnaws at him, leaving him with a pervasive sense of guilt and an overwhelming desire to isolate himself from potential dangers. On weekends, John avoids going on drives or even riding as a passenger in cars; he fears that another accident is inevitable. His hobbies—hiking and traveling—which once brought him joy, now seem fraught with risk. The only time he feels relatively at ease is when Sarah stays home with him, ensuring his environment remains under control. Recently, John has begun to experience intense flashbacks while driving in the city where the accident occurred. Even a similar model of car passing by can trigger a visceral reaction; he clutches the steering wheel tightly and stares intently ahead, almost as if willing himself not to crash again. These episodes have led him to drive longer routes to avoid certain streets, increasing his travel time significantly. Despite his best efforts to push through, John’s daily life is marred by hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors that affect nearly every aspect of his routine. The financial analyst who once prided himself on his ability to assess risks now finds himself paralyzed by the fear of what could happen next. While Sarah remains supportive, she struggles with understanding the depth of his trauma. John’s life continues to be defined by a haunting sense of insecurity and an unwavering fear that another accident is just around the corner. His daily routines and interactions are shadowed by the traumatic event, leaving him navigating a delicate balance between his professional responsibilities and personal safety concerns.
